sentences.text: He said it on the eighth of December, in the kitchen, at about nine at night, and he said it badly.
What he said was that he hated it.
He had not planned to.
He had come down for a glass of milk.
His mother had asked him a completely ordinary question about a form for a trip, and he had heard himself start talking and had been, for about the first thirty seconds, as surprised as she was.
He said he hated the bus and the shop shutting at four and that there was nothing, there was actually nothing, there was one shop.
He said everybody had known each other since they were three and that they were not unkind about it and that was somehow worse.
He said he had been at that school for four months and had not once been to anybody's house.
He said that when they had left he had told everyone at his old school he'd be back at Christmas and that he had known when he said it that it was not true.
He said that everyone kept telling him he was settling in beautifully and that he had no idea who had told them that, because it had not been him.
His mother did not say it would come good.

She sat at the table and let him finish and then she said, "I know," and then, after a while, "I don't know what to do about most of that." Which was, Tam thought later, the first accurate sentence anybody had said to him since August.
They talked for about two hours.
Nothing was solved.
The shop still shut at four.
He did not see the fox in December at all.
He noticed the absence about ten days in, on the way home on the bus, going past the wall by the turning where it had been every second Tuesday since October.
It was an odd feeling and not a good one at first.
He had spent three months wanting it to stop and it had stopped, and the stopping did not feel like winning.
It felt like the end of something he had been having a conversation with.
He looked.

He is not going to pretend he did not look — he checked the garden from the landing window every night for three weeks like an idiot, and there was the shed and the grass and the wheelie bin and nothing else.
He saw it once more, in the following June, on a Tuesday, from the bus.

It was on the wall by the turning to the caravan site, sitting, front legs straight, and by then he was fourteen and had been to Effie's house fourteen times and was in the football, and he was not in the least lost, and he looked at it all the way past and it looked back.
He has thought about that one for years.
The version he has settled on is that it was not there for him at all.
There were about thirty people on that bus.

But he is not certain, and the other possibility has never entirely gone away, which is that you do not stop being somebody who arrived from somewhere else, and that the fox knows this, and that once in a while it sits on a wall in the sunshine to remind you.
He is twenty-six now and he lives in Fernaig, which nobody who knew him at thirteen would have predicted, including him.
